name: Gyeongju
info: Gyeongju is a coastal city in the far south-east of North Gyeongsang Province, South Korea, founded by tradition in 57 BCE as the capital of the kingdom of Silla, which it remained for close to a thousand years.

facts.founded: According to Korean records, probably based on the dynastic chronicles of Silla, the state of Saro-guk was established in 57 BCE when six small villages in the Gyeongju area united under Bak Hyeokgeose, the first ruler of Silla.
facts.where: On the banks of the Hyeongsan River in the Gyeongju Basin, in the far south-eastern corner of North Gyeongsang Province in South Korea, with the Sea of Japan to the east.
facts.known: Capital of Silla; Sŏrabŏl; the Silla court and its tombs; Bulguksa and Seokguram; the Cheomseongdae observatory; the Hwarang; Gukhak, the national academy of 682; birthplace of Cheondoism
facts.today: Gyeongju is a city of North Gyeongsang Province in South Korea, an urban and rural complex formed in 1995 when the city and the surrounding county were united.

t: Gyeongju was the capital of Silla from the kingdom's traditional founding in 57 BCE until its surrender in 935, and after the unification of the peninsula up to the Taedong River in 668 it was the centre of Korean political and cultural life.
Under Goryeo and Joseon it lost its national standing, though it kept a place as a regional centre until the provincial capital passed to Daegu in 1601.
Many of its buildings and sculptures were damaged by invasions and by Neo-Confucian radicals, and the tombs and Buddhist sites that survive are the main record of the Silla city.
dyk: The name Sŏrabŏl, by which Gyeongju was known in the Silla period, eventually evolved into a Korean word for a capital city, as in Seoul.

sections.origins:
Gyeongju lies in the far south-eastern corner of North Gyeongsang Province, in the Gyeongsang Basin. Its historic centre stands on the banks of the Hyeongsan River, low mountains that are outliers of the Taebaek range are scattered around it, and to the east lies the coast of the Sea of Japan. Prehistoric remains including Mumun pottery have been excavated in central Gyeongju and in several villages of the surrounding districts, dolmens are found in several places, and Bronze Age relics and graveyards represent the Samhan confederacy period, from around the 1st century BCE to the 3rd century CE.

The city first enters non-Korean records as Saro-guk, one of twelve petty states of the Jinhan confederacy in the Samhan period. Korean records, probably based on the dynastic chronicles of Silla, say that Saro-guk was established in 57 BCE, when six small villages in the Gyeongju area united under Bak Hyeokgeose, the first ruler of the kingdom. As the kingdom expanded, it changed its name to Silla. In the Silla period the city was called Sŏrabŏl, a name assumed to mean capital, and also Gyerim, literally Rooster's forest, and Geumseong, City of Gold or Metal, that is, an impenetrable fortress. Sŏrabŏl eventually evolved into a Korean word for a capital city, as in Seoul.
sections.growth:
After the unification of the peninsula up to the Taedong River in 668, Gyeongju became the centre of Korean political and cultural life. It was home to the Silla court and to the great majority of the kingdom's elite, and Silla ruled about two-thirds of the Korean peninsula at its height between the 7th and 9th centuries. The city's prosperity was reported as far away as Persia in the 9th-century Book of Roads and Kingdoms. The Samguk yusa gives the city's population in its peak period as 178,936 households, which suggests a total population of almost one million. Many of Gyeongju's most famous sites date from this Unified Silla period.

Commerce and trade developed early. The Samguk sagi records the establishment of Gyeongdosi, a market for the capital area, in March 490 in the reign of King Soji, and of Dongsi, the East Market, in 509 in the reign of King Jijeung. Formal education also has a long history in the city: the Gukhak, or national academy, was established there in 682, at the beginning of the Unified Silla period, with a curriculum focused on the Confucian classics for local officials. It closed after the fall of Silla in the 10th century.
sections.rulers:
Gyeongju was the capital of the kingdom of Silla, dated from 57 BCE to 935, for close to one thousand years. In the late 9th century the kingdom declined and fell apart, giving way to the Later Three Kingdoms. In 927 Gyeongju was pillaged by Hubaekje, one of these kingdoms, and in 935 King Gyeongsun surrendered his title and country to Taejo, who had established the Goryeo dynasty. The title of capital went to Gaegyeong, present-day Kaesong.

In 940 King Taejo gave the city the name Gyeongju, which literally means Congratulatory district. In 987, when Goryeo established three additional capitals in politically important provinces, Gyeongju was designated Donggyeong, the East Capital, but the title was removed in 1012, the third year of King Hyeongjong's reign, because of political rivalries. The city was made the seat of Yeongnam Province, with jurisdiction over a wide area, and for much of the Goryeo period it was also the seat of the Andong Daedohobu, the Great Protectorate of the East, which oversaw military affairs for much of eastern and central Korea. It lost that distinction in the 13th century, after bloody rebellions connected with a Silla restoration movement broke out in the area, and its boundaries were greatly reduced.

Under the Joseon dynasty Gyeongju was no longer of national importance but remained a regional centre. The Great Yeongnam Road, which linked Seoul to Dongnae without passing near it, became the chief artery of Gyeongsang Province, and in 1601 the provincial capital passed to Daegu.
sections.life:
As the capital of Silla, Gyeongju was a centre of culture, and most of the kingdom's leading figures lived there: rulers, scholars such as Seol Chong and Ch'oe Ch'i-wŏn, and generals such as Kim Yu-sin, leader of the Hwarang warriors. The Hwarang were a military cadet of youths from the aristocratic class, trained in academic and martial arts on the basis of Buddhism and patriotism, and several of Silla's greatest generals came from them. Silla's patronage of Buddhism left the temple of Bulguksa, the grotto of Seokguram and many Buddhas and Bodhisattvas carved on the mountainsides, particularly on Namsan, and the ruins of Hwangnyongsa, said to have been Korea's largest temple. The Cheomseongdae is one of the oldest surviving astronomical observatories in East Asia.

The great tombs of the Silla kings and elite stand in the middle of the city, where there are 35 royal tombs and 155 tumuli, and the tombs of Geumgwanchong, Seobongchong and Cheonmachong have given artefacts that are good examples of Silla culture. Under Joseon, Gyeongju joined the rest of Gyeongsang in becoming a hotbed of the conservative Sarim faction, and several seowon, private Confucian academies, were set up in the city. In the 1830s Gyeongju had five five-day markets, and its village market was counted among the two leading markets of the Yeongnam area. The city is also the birthplace of Cheondoism, which grew from the Donghak disciplines established by Choe Je-u.
sections.crises:
The historic centre of Gyeongju lies on low ground on the Hyeongsan River and has been flooded repeatedly, often by typhoons. The chronicles report a major flood on average every 27.9 years, beginning in the 1st century, and modern flood control brought a sharp fall in flooding in the later 20th century. The last major flood occurred in 1991, when the Deokdong Lake reservoir overflowed in Typhoon Gladys.

The city suffered numerous assaults over the centuries. In 927 it was pillaged by Hubaekje. In the 13th century Mongol forces destroyed a nine-story wooden pagoda at Hwangnyongsa, and during the Imjin War of 1592 to 1598 the area became a heated battlefield and Japanese forces burned the wooden structures at Bulguksa. Not all the damage came from invasions: in the early Joseon period Neo-Confucian radicals hacked the arms and heads off many Buddhist sculptures on Namsan.

After liberation in 1945 the Gyeongju area became notorious for guerrilla activity in the mountains. Most of the city was spared in the Korean War and stayed under South Korean control, but for a brief time in late 1950 portions of it stood on the front lines, as North Korean forces pushed the Pusan Perimeter southward from Pohang. An earthquake of magnitude 5.8 struck in September 2015, and no major damage or injuries were reported.
sections.legacy:
Gyeongju is often called the museum without walls, because so many archaeological sites and cultural properties from the Silla period remain in it. A museum, the forerunner of the Gyeongju National Museum, was set up in 1915 to show the finds from the tombs, which had remained largely intact over the centuries and were excavated in the early 20th century, largely by Japanese archaeologists. Their work is often accused of recklessness and plunder, although others take a more neutral view, and few excavation reports were published. The museum now holds 16,333 artefacts, and the city has 31 National Treasures. Seokguram and Bulguksa were the first Korean sites included on the UNESCO World Heritage List, in 1995.

For most of the 20th century the city was relatively small and no longer ranked among the major cities of Korea. It became a railway junction in the later years of the Japanese occupation, and the steel mill at Pohang and the chemical complex at Ulsan, both begun in 1973, helped to support the growth of its own manufacturing sector. The city was united with the surrounding county in 1995 and is today an urban and rural complex of 23 administrative districts, with a population of about 264,000. The Gyeongju dialect, which it shares with northern parts of Ulsan, has been treated by some linguists as keeping vestiges of the Silla language.

summary: Gyeongju, in the far south-east of South Korea, was the capital of Silla, traditionally from 57 BCE to 935, and the centre of Korean political and cultural life after 668. It declined under Goryeo and Joseon, and its tombs, temples and sculptures remain the record of the Silla city.
notes: START: -57 with circa true; the date is that of Korean records 'probably based on the dynastic chronicles of Silla', so it is traditional. The articles give no archaeological founding date for the city itself; Mumun pottery and dolmens show earlier habitation of the area.

SILLA'S END and Goryeo's dates disagree: the main article gives Silla as 57 BC to 935 AD but also says Unified Silla 'ended in the beginning of 10th century by Goryeo (918-1392)'; the history article has Goryeo founded 918 and Goryeo dynasty (935-1392). I used 935 for the surrender (both articles) and left out Goryeo's start and end years.

POPULATION: the main article says Samguk yusa gives more than 170,000 households or 800,000 to 900,000 inhabitants, and also 178,936 households (almost one million), and elsewhere that the city had an estimated million residents at the peak. The history article gives 178,936. I used 178,936 households only and omitted the 800,000-900,000 figure, the million and the claim that it was the fourth largest city in the world (stated flatly in the main article, unsourced).
Present population: the main article gives 264,091 in December 2012, the history article 269,343 in the 2008 census. I wrote 'about 264,000' without a year.

Names: the main article spells Bak Hyeokgeose, the history article Bak Hyeokgose; I used the former. Geumseong is glossed 'City of Gold or Metal i.e. impenetrable fortress' in one, 'City of Gold' (金成) in the other.
Hwarang: the article says the system declined after Silla and was disbanded in the Joseon period; left out of the text for space. Gukhak 682 is in the main article only.

Excavations: the history article says they were largely carried out by Japanese archaeologists and are accused of recklessness and plunder, 'although others take a more neutral view'; I kept that hedge.
Imjin War 1592-1598 is named in the history article; the main article says only 'Japanese invasions of Korea'.

Left out as not history or not allowed: tourism, sports, economy, cuisine, government, twin cities, the nuclear plant, hospitals, the 2021 find of remains of human sacrifices at Wolseong Palace (a recent announcement; could be added as 'a 1,500-year-old female skeleton found at the western wall of Wolseong Palace').
